description: A team of two passionate innovators combining Product Management, UX Design, technology and storytelling to tackle one of humanity's greatest challenges: exploring beyond Earth. Our mission is to bridge Earth and space, transforming complex planetary data into meaningful insights that help identify terrestrial environments analogous to the Moon and Mars. We believe innovation isn't about the size of the team. It's about the ambition of the vision. Two women. One planet. Infinite possibilities.
summary:
Parallax finds the place on Earth whose terrain behaves most like a given place on the Moon or Mars, so teams can rehearse a mission where it matters. A team describes the test it needs (rover mobility, navigation, drilling) and Parallax searches 42,405 Earth windows of 50 km built from NASA elevation data, explains why each one passes or is excluded, and lists what is still unknown.

We also turned the challenge around and mapped the Moon and Mars from Earth. Earth has a strong terrain twin for the whole lunar south polar cap and 99.9% of Mars, including all nine Artemis III candidate regions. 20 of our 21 Earth twins are new analog sites: none of 57 listed analogs lies within 100 km. Every test was pre-registered and checked against sites agencies already use.

Parallax then plans the field campaign: the closest twin near an airport, the months a team can work there, where to sleep, and a printable sheet with altitude, nearest hospital and emergency numbers. It is also honest about where the analogy breaks: gravity, vacuum, temperature and rock. The question is no longer whether a place can be rehearsed on Earth, but where.
details:
What it does

Before a rover, an instrument or a crew goes to the Moon or Mars, it is tested on Earth. Choosing where is still largely a matter of experience and a few well-known sites. Parallax turns that choice into an explicit, traceable search.

  • Experiment first. A team starts from a test profile (rover mobility, navigation, drilling, ISRU) and measurable limits such as slope and land cover. Free text is kept in the report but never drives selection.
  • Measured candidates. Parallax ranks Earth regions by how closely their terrain behaves like the target, explains why each passes or is excluded, and lists the evidence still missing.
  • All of Earth, with terrain conditions. The search covers 42,405 Earth windows, every 50 km from 56° S to 60° N, against Jezero, Shackleton or any of the nine Artemis III candidate regions. A team can require bare ground, little vegetation, an access band, permafrost, rock like the reference or temperatures like the destination. Each condition only removes windows, never reorders them, and a window without the value does not pass.
  • Where, and when. For lunar targets, a lunar light calendar shows the days and hours over the next 12 months when the Sun over each Earth candidate sits as low as at the lunar south pole (0–1.6°), the grazing light that makes Artemis navigation and imaging hard.
  • The reverse map. For every 50 km of the lunar south polar cap and of Mars, Parallax shows its closest Earth twin; for any place on Earth, it shows the Moon and Mars "under your feet".
  • Plan the campaign. For each Moon and Mars destination, the closest strong twin within 100 km of an airport with scheduled flights and ten distinct fallback sites; when to go (workable months from NASA POWER) and where to sleep (OpenStreetMap); and a printable three-page campaign sheet in English and Spanish: altitude and acclimatization, daylight, nearest hospital, fuel and food, road access, emergency numbers, 14 field checks and three fallback sites.
  • Team verification. What Parallax cannot measure (permits, logistics, field measurements) stays marked "verification required". The campaign team records who checked each item, when and against what source; the candidate then shows as verified by the team. This is declared by the team, not certified by Parallax, and it never changes the ranking. Verifications travel in the exported JSON.

Source code on GitHub

All code, frozen pre-registration rules (config/), validation results (results/, docs/) and tests. https://github.com/marminguez/Parallax

How it works

  1. Reference fingerprint. Slopes are computed on a 1 km grid inside a 50 × 50 km window around the planetary site (Jezero crater on Mars; Shackleton crater and the nine Artemis III regions on the Moon) and binned into a slope histogram.
  2. Earth windows. The same window and grid are built on Earth from NASA SRTMGL30 elevation. NASA MOD44W excludes water: a window needs at least 90 % land.
  3. Similarity. Windows are ranked by the Jensen–Shannon distance between slope histograms. Lower means more similar terrain behaviour; it is not a suitability percentage.
  4. Earth constraints. For Mars targets, the share of bare ground from ESA WorldCover is added to the score. Five conditions measured on every Earth window (bare ground and vegetation, access, permafrost, rock family, surface temperature) can then filter the results, and topsoil texture (SoilGrids 2.0) adds minimum sand, maximum clay and maximum coarse fragments; they never change the order.
  5. Presentation. Results are labelled with place names and grouped into independent sites. Neither step changes the ranking.

Every run records its request, dataset versions and file hashes, and can be exported as JSON.

How we know it works

All tests were pre-registered: the site lists and predictions were committed to the repository before Parallax evaluated them, and no known analog was used to build the model.
Established analogs fall, at the median, among the closest ~19 % of Earth to their target. The hyperarid core of the Atacama Desert is closer to Jezero than every sampled Earth window. All nine Artemis III candidate regions have a strong Earth twin, in mountain ranges of Pakistan, Peru, Iran, Argentina and Canada. With a rule fixed before computing, we checked each twin against the 57 listed analogs of three lists (agency-used sites, Apollo training sites, Analog Atlas): 20 of the 21 have none within 100 km, so they are new analog candidates, not rediscovered ones. The exception is Holden crater's twin near Doğubayazıt (Türkiye), 47 km from Armash, where AMADEE-24 was run. The twin of Nobile Rim 1 (Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan) is closer to its lunar target than any of the 18 agency-used analogs are to theirs. The few Mars windows Earth struggles to imitate are the obvious giants: Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

We also report what did not work. Two of our three pre-registered predictions for the reverse map failed: we expected the lunar south pole to be harder to imitate than Mars, and it was not.

Where the analogy breaks

Each twin is also characterized on six more dimensions, with verdicts fixed before computing. This is descriptive: it never changes a twin.

  • Fine relief at 60 m (Copernicus GLO-30 vs LOLA 20 m): all ten lunar twins behave like the Moon at 50 km but not at 60 m. Earth's mountains, carved by water and ice, have 42–85 % of their slopes at 15° or more; the Moon has 13–48 %. Jezero's twin holds partly. So we then searched at fine scale: with rules and three predictions fixed before computing, we measured 60 m relief for the 538 windows teams see most (the top of each reference and the twins). Only 0.17 % of the lunar pairs hold at 60 m, yet every lunar reference has candidates that hold or partly hold; 9 pairs hold, for Nobile Rim 1, Slater Plain, Malapert Massif, Shackleton and Mons Mouton. For Jezero, 26 of its top 50 hold or partly hold. All three predictions held, and a team can now require fine relief as a search condition.
  • Soil texture (0–5 cm, SoilGrids 2.0): for rover and drilling tests, what the ground is made of matters, not only whether it is bare. With rules, two checks and three predictions fixed before reading a single value, we measured topsoil sand, silt, clay and coarse fragments on all 42,405 windows from ISRIC's 1 km maps. Both checks passed and two predictions held (42,401 windows measured; bare windows are slightly sandier, 48 % vs 44 %). One failed: we expected bare ground to lack soil data because SoilGrids masks bare surface, but the 1 km maps cover it fully, so there the values are model predictions with few field observations behind them. We publish that result and say it on every candidate sheet. Soil describes Earth only: the Moon and Mars have no comparable map, so it carries no verdict and never changes the order.
  • Surface temperature (NASA POWER): the lunar twins cover 13–35 % of the Moon's surface temperature range; the Moon gets 149–203 °C colder. Eight of the eleven Mars twins never reach Martian ground temperatures; only Jezero's twin, in the southern Urals, covers most of the Mars range.
  • Access (NASA SEDAC population density): 4 twins are remote, 10 rural and 7 populated.
  • Ice (LOLA permanent shadow, NASA SWIM, Gruber permafrost index): every lunar region studied holds cold traps (1.5–22 % of the window in permanent shadow), but only two lunar twins have permafrost: those of Nobile Rim 1 and Malapert Massif, both in the Karakoram (Pakistan). Among the 21 twins, those are the ones to rehearse drilling ice-bearing ground for Artemis; across all of Earth there are many more (below). It rehearses digging frozen ground, not the Moon's −200 °C cold. On Mars, only Viking 2 (Utopia Planitia) shows clear ice. The Mars rule was amended after seeing the first results, because SWIM defines values near 0 as inconclusive; both versions are published.
  • Bare ground (ESA WorldCover): at 50 km the Moon and Mars are loose ground everywhere, yet 16 of the 21 twins are mostly vegetated. Shape alone is not enough. Only three hold: Opportunity's twin in the Sahara (Arlit, Niger; 98 % bare) and the two Karakoram twins of Malapert Massif and Nobile Rim 1. Mars Pathfinder's twin is rainforest in French Guiana. This is why Parallax's experiment search adds a bare-ground filter. The analogy is about open, loose ground, never about lunar or Martian dust itself.
  • Rock family (GLiM; USGS Geologic Map of Mars): same shape, different rock. No lunar twin has the Moon's anorthosite or gabbro. On Mars, two twins hold: Viking 2's lowland plains against sediments near Roma, Australia, and Jezero's sedimentary unit against mixed sedimentary rock in the southern Urals. Holden's twin, by Mount Ararat (Türkiye), is 47 % basalt.

From 21 twins to all of Earth

We then measured five of these dimensions (bare ground, access, permafrost, rock family and surface temperature) on all 42,405 eligible Earth windows, with the rules and four predictions registered before computing. Before measuring any new window, the code had to reproduce the published values of the 21 twins exactly, and the web search had to give the same distances as the Python engine. All four predictions held:

  • 18.5 % of windows are mostly bare ground (predicted 5–20 %).
  • 4.2 % have permafrost (predicted under 15 %).
  • 29.5 % are remote (predicted 20–40 %).
  • 111 of Shackleton's 1,769 strong twins combine bare ground and permafrost (predicted at least 5). Almost all are in High Asia (Xinjiang, Ladakh, Tibet, the Pamir), with one in Catamarca, Argentina. Among the 21 twins we had found two; now a team has more than a hundred candidates to rehearse drilling into frozen, open ground for Artemis. The permafrost value is a zonation index, not measured ground ice, so each site needs a field check.

Each of the nine Artemis III regions is now a search reference too, with its own pre-registered check and prediction. With no conditions, each region's first result is the twin already published on the reverse map. With bare ground and permafrost required, every region has between 63 (Nobile Rim 1) and 170 (Slater Plain) candidates among its strong twins; we predicted at least 5 for 7 of the 9 regions, and it held for all 9. From each region's sheet in Missions, one click opens that search.

From twin to campaign

A twin is only useful if a team can get there. With rules fixed before computing, Parallax looks through every strong twin of each destination for the closest one within 100 km of an airport with scheduled flights. It never changes a reverse-map twin.

  • 10 of the 21 reverse-map twins are already reachable. The other 11 all get a reachable strong twin: Nobile Rim 1 moves from Gilgit-Baltistan (Pakistan) to Vicuña (Chile), Opportunity from Arlit (Niger) to Deming (New Mexico, USA), Shackleton from Tibet to Chao (Peru).
  • Workable months (lows ≥ −10 °C, highs ≤ 35 °C, rain ≤ 3 mm/day): the reachable twin is easier to work in 6 of the 11 cases. Vicuña works 11 months a year against 3 for the Pakistan twin; Chao works all year.
  • The rule also says no. Four reachable Mars twins, among them Jezero's in Namibia, and several original twins in the hot tropics have no month that meets it: monthly highs above 35 °C, or more than 3 mm/day of rain all year in Papua New Guinea. We publish that rather than relax the rule.
  • Where to sleep: Vicuña has 113 places to stay within 50 km, the nearest 1 km away; six original twins have none mapped.
  • Facts on the ground (rules fixed before computing): Nobile Rim 1's Pakistan twin sits at a median 4,739 m, Vicuña's at 2,545 m with a road 0.7 km from the centre and a hospital 25 km away. Shackleton's twin in Tibet is at 4,502 m; its reachable twin at Chao (Peru) at 1,117 m. Viking 2's twin near Roma (Australia) has no hospital mapped within 100 km.
  • Paperwork: the team enters its nationalities, and each site shows the entry rule for every passport, the country's travel-risk level and the permits needed to do research there, each with its source. Researched for every country of the twins and reachable twins. It changes the choice: Nobile Rim 1's Pakistan twin and Shackleton's Tibet twin need border or military permits, Opportunity's in Niger a military escort, while their reachable twins in Chile, the USA and Peru need none of that.

Who it is for

  • Mission and analog teams: agencies, scientists and analog campaigns looking for where to test habitats, rovers and procedures.
  • Education and outreach: schools, museums and planetariums. A public page and a QR code answer "what Moon, and what Mars, is under your feet?"; location stays on the visitor's device.
  • Geotourism: places that want to know which part of the Moon or Mars they resemble, for science outreach and analog tourism.

What we hope to achieve

We want site selection for Moon and Mars rehearsals to become a measured, reproducible decision that any team can repeat and challenge. Next steps: finer-scale terrain so crater-scale analogs become visible, polar coverage (Devon Island, Svalbard), one field site that serves several rehearsals at once (a single campaign for more than one Moon or Mars target), and field measurements to close each gap the campaign sheet lists.

Known limits

  • Windows are 50 × 50 km on a 1 km grid: this is regional pre-selection, not obstacle-scale or wheel-safety analysis.
  • Twins are ranked on terrain shape only. Temperature, access, ice, bare ground and rock family are characterized afterwards and never change a twin (in the experiment search they only act as filters); mineralogy, dust properties and radiation are not measured. Earth coverage runs from 56° S to 60° N.
  • Earth cannot reproduce reduced gravity, the Moon's vacuum, Mars's thin atmosphere or space radiation. Parallax finds terrain that behaves alike, never a place that is "like being on the Moon". Passing every filter does not qualify a site for NASA; all candidates stay provisional.
  • Campaign logistics are descriptive. Airport distances are straight lines, not roads; workable months use monthly means, so a hot month may still be workable early in the day; OpenStreetMap may be incomplete. Altitude, hospitals and road access are measured from the window centre; 3 of 627 values could not be computed and are shown as missing. Road condition is not checked. Entry rules, permits and safety are researched only for the twins' countries (14 Nov 2026) and they change: each team confirms them with the embassy.

Tools and languages

Python 3 (NumPy, rasterio/GDAL, pyproj, pandas, PyYAML, pytest) for the analysis engine; TypeScript with Next.js, React, MapLibre GL JS and Tailwind CSS for the web application. All open-source software. No special hardware.

Full documentation

The Parallax Book (36 pages) covers the method, all pre-registered validations (including the predictions that failed), the reverse map, the six analog dimensions, campaign planning, limits and a technical annex with every frozen rule and the commands to reproduce each result: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1L12m4oErbs1irqXIdYu5iJflqYGMA8nJ/view?usp=sharing

Use of AI

We used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and writing assistant: to help write and test parts of the Python engine and the Next.js application, and to draft and translate documentation. AI-assisted commits carry a co-author line in the repository. Every result was reviewed by the team, and every number comes from code run on the data listed below. AI plays no part in how Parallax ranks or classifies places: the ranking is a deterministic Jensen–Shannon distance between measured slope distributions, and no model is trained. The animated illustrations in the demo deck were generated as code with Claude and are labelled as SI-generated on each slide. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers were generated or modified with AI.
